transcript.content: Hello, welcome in—I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I suppose what brings me in is… I’ve noticed this past year or so that I’m just always doing something. Puttering around, fixing little things, rearranging, saying yes to one more volunteer job—nothing terrible, I don’t think—but even at my age, I seem to have a hard time just sitting down and being still. I wasn’t sure if that was worth coming in for, but I thought maybe I should ask.
Over this past year, have you noticed that you need less sleep than you used to, yet still feel fine and energetic the next day?

No, I don’t think so. My sleep seems… about what I’d expect, I suppose. I can have nights where I’m up and down a bit, but I wouldn’t say I need less sleep and feel wonderfully energetic the next day or anything like that. Does that answer it the way you mean?
Along with this need to keep busy, have you also noticed yourself worrying a lot—about things like health, family, or everyday matters—more than you used to?

I don’t think so, not especially. I mean, I worry the normal amount, I suppose—family things, health here and there—but I wouldn’t say it’s more than before or that it’s the main reason I’m keeping busy. Is that what you’re asking?
Have you noticed any unexplained weight loss, feeling unusually warm or sweaty, a racing heart, or trembling hands over this past year?

No, I don’t believe so. I haven’t noticed weight loss or feeling hot and sweaty like that, and I don’t think my heart’s been racing or my hands trembling. At least, nothing that’s stood out to me. Is that helpful?
Thinking back to when you were a child or teenager, were you ever especially restless, fidgety, or unable to sit still compared to other kids your age?

Yes… I suppose I was, though I don’t want to make it sound worse than it was. In grade school I do remember being scolded for getting up out of my seat, or talking over other children. Teachers would say I was “too lively,” things like that. That was before I was a teenager, yes. Is that the sort of thing you mean?

Between your school years and this past year, did you continue to notice this restlessness and difficulty sitting still throughout your adult life, or was there a long stretch—say, your 30s, 40s, or 50s—when you didn't have this issue?

I’m not sure I can trace it that neatly, honestly. I don’t remember there being some long period where I thought, “Oh, that’s gone,” but I also wasn’t really paying attention to it in those terms. I’ve tended to keep myself busy, but I suppose I just thought of that as my way of being, not necessarily a problem.

So… I don’t know if that answers it properly. I can’t point to a clear stretch where it completely stopped.

Would you say this constant busyness or restlessness has caused problems for you—like trouble at work, in relationships, or with things you need to get done—or has it mostly just been a personality trait that hasn't really caused difficulties?

Well… I’d like to say it’s mostly just my personality, and maybe a lot of the time it is. But I suppose there have been a few awkward moments.

At the senior center, after meetings, I’ve had to apologize because I came across too strong or got people a bit stirred up. And one friend—very kindly—suggested maybe I should take a smaller role at the sign-up table, because my manner was making things tense. I felt badly about that.

So, not terrible problems, I don’t think, but yes… it has caused some difficulty. Is that the kind of example you mean?

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports chronic, pervasive restlessness and inability to sit still beginning in childhood (grade school, before age 12), with continued difficulty across adulthood into the present. Symptoms are primarily hyperactive/impulsive in nature (fidgeting, excessive activity, interrupting/overstepping in social interactions) rather than primarily inattentive. There is evidence of functional impairment (social friction at senior center, being asked to step back from a role due to interpersonal tension). Anxiety-related worry, hyperthyroid symptoms, and manic-spectrum decreased need for sleep were explicitly denied, making GAD, hyperthyroidism, and bipolar disorder less likely. The chronic, early-onset, trait-like course without discrete episodic mood elevation supports a diagnosis of ADHD, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation, persisting into late adulthood.
